name: Generic
description: A starting point for any game: core gameplay, levels and UI, each with the tech and assets it needs. Add the features specific to your game next to them.

pillars.name: Core Fantasy
pillars.feeling: the one experience the whole game is built to deliver

pillars.name: Moment-to-Moment Fun
pillars.feeling: what makes the next ten seconds enjoyable

pillars.name: Reason to Return
pillars.feeling: why the player comes back tomorrow

gameExamples.heading: Pitch
gameExamples.text: A short, replayable game where every session ends with the player wanting one more go.

gameExamples.heading: Core Loop
gameExamples.text:
1. Pick a goal for the session.
2. Play the core mechanic to reach it.
3. Earn a reward.
4. Spend it to unlock a new option.

docs.title: Core Gameplay
docs.summary: What the player does over and over: the core loop's mechanics and rules.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can understand the goal of a session within a minute.
- As a player, I can play the core mechanic in different ways.
- As a player, I can see my progress toward the session's goal.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text:
- A clear goal at the start.
- Feedback on every success and failure.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- A session lasts 10-20 minutes.
- Losing keeps some progress so the next attempt starts ahead.

docs.title: Gameplay Framework
docs.summary: Game mode, player controller and pawn, and how the core loop runs in code.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: The game mode sets the rules of a session, the player controller turns input into actions, and the pawn is what the player controls. Game state holds what everyone needs to know about the match.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `AProjectGameMode`: starts and ends sessions, spawns players
- `AProjectPlayerController`: input mapping and UI
- `AProjectCharacter`: the player's pawn
- `AProjectGameState`: session state everyone can read

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Input actions and mapping contexts.
- Session rules (time limit, win condition) in a data asset.

docs.title: Characters
docs.summary: Player and NPC meshes, rigs and animations.

examples.heading: Assets Needed
examples.text:
| Asset | Type | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Player character mesh | Mesh | Placeholder | To source |
| Player animation set | Animation | Placeholder | To source |
| NPC meshes | Mesh | Placeholder | To source |
| Shared skeleton | Rig | Placeholder | To source |

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Readable silhouettes and slightly exaggerated proportions so characters read from the gameplay camera.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- Characters on the engine's standard skeleton (or retargetable to it).
- Modular outfits that share one skeleton.
- Animation packs with locomotion, combat and reactions.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text:
- Characters with very different levels of detail side by side.
- Rigs that can't be retargeted.
- Hyper-realistic faces next to stylized bodies.

docs.title: Levels
docs.summary: Where the player plays, and what they can do and see there.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can move through each level and always know where to go next.
- As a player, I can find side paths that reward curiosity.
- As a player, I can see where I've been and where I haven't.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text:
- Landmarks visible from far away.
- Light and color that guide me toward the main path.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Every level has a clear start, goal and one optional reward.
- Levels teach a new idea before testing it.

docs.title: Level Streaming
docs.summary: How levels load, stream and transition.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Each level is a persistent level with streamed sublevels; World Partition loads cells around the player. Transitions between levels go through a loading screen that waits for the next level to be ready.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `ULevelTransitionSubsystem`: loads the next level behind a loading screen
- `World Partition data layers`: what loads where

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Streaming distances per cell size.
- The level list and their loading screens in a data asset.

docs.title: Environment Art
docs.summary: Meshes, materials, props and lighting setups the levels are built from.

examples.heading: Assets Needed
examples.text:
| Asset | Type | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Modular kit (walls, floors, stairs) | Mesh | Placeholder | To source |
| Props | Mesh | Placeholder | To source |
| Materials and textures | Material | Placeholder | To source |
| Lighting presets | Lighting | Placeholder | To source |

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: One consistent material language: the same texel density, wear and color palette across every kit.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- Modular kits built on a grid.
- Packs with Nanite-ready meshes and trim sheets.
- Prop packs from the same artist as the kit.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text:
- Mixing kits from different artists in one area.
- Photoscanned assets next to hand-painted ones.
- Props at a different scale from the kit.

docs.title: UI
docs.summary: Menus and HUD: what the player sees and can do outside the game world.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can start, pause and quit from clear menus.
- As a player, I can change graphics, audio and control settings.
- As a player, I can see the information I need during play without it covering the action.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text:
- A title screen, pause menu and settings screens.
- A HUD with only what matters right now.
- Button prompts that match my input device.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Every screen can be used with a gamepad as well as mouse and keyboard.
- Pausing stops gameplay time.
- Settings save immediately.

docs.title: UI Framework
docs.summary: How screens and widgets are built, opened, navigated and fed data.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Screens are UMG widgets pushed onto a stack by a UI manager subsystem. The top screen gets input; popping it returns to the one below. Gameplay talks to the HUD through events, never directly.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `UProjectUISubsystem`: owns the screen stack and opens and closes screens
- `UScreenWidget`: base class for every full screen (menus, settings)
- `UHUDWidget`: the in-game HUD; listens to gameplay events

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Screen classes and their input modes in a data asset.
- Settings in the game user settings, saved per user.

docs.title: UI Art
docs.summary: Icons, fonts, panels and widget skins.

examples.heading: Assets Needed
examples.text:
| Asset | Type | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Icons | UI | Placeholder | To source |
| Fonts (headings, body) | UI | Placeholder | To source |
| Panel and button skins | UI | Placeholder | To source |
| Input prompt icons | UI | Placeholder | To source |

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Clean and readable first: flat shapes, high contrast, one accent color. Icons share one line weight and perspective.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- UI kits with matching icons, buttons and panels.
- Fonts licensed for games, with the character sets we localize to.
- Input prompt packs covering keyboard, Xbox and PlayStation.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text:
- Mixing icon packs with different styles.
- Ornate frames that crowd the screen.
- Fonts that are hard to read at small sizes.

docs.title: Music and Sound
docs.summary: Music, sound effects and ambience, and where each is used.

examples.heading: Assets Needed
examples.text:
| Asset | Type | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Main theme | Music | Placeholder | To source |
| Gameplay loops | Music | Placeholder | To source |
| UI sounds (click, back, confirm) | Sound | Placeholder | To source |
| Ambience beds | Sound | Placeholder | To source |

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Music sets the mood of each area; sound effects are short and punchy so they read over the music.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- Music packs with loopable stems.
- Sound effect libraries with variations of each sound.
- Licenses that allow commercial use and streaming.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text:
- Tracks that don't loop cleanly.
- Effects with long tails that muddy fast moments.
- Mixing many libraries with different loudness.

docs.title: Save and Load
docs.summary: What persists between sessions, how it's stored, and how saves stay compatible.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: A save game object holds everything that persists. Systems register what they need saved; saving serializes it to a slot, loading restores it before the level starts. Saves carry a version number so old saves can be migrated.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `USaveSubsystem`: saves and loads slots, runs migrations
- `UProjectSaveGame`: the saved data, with a version field
- `ISaveable`: interface for systems that write and read their part

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Save slots in the platform's save location.
- A version number per save, bumped on every breaking change.
